extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy, constitutional theorists, and citizens considering legitimacy of government power
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and explains criteria for legitimate executive, parental, political, and despotical powers, and the moral-legal limits of prerogative and conquest in forming government authority. Focuses on when discretionary power is justified, who may be judged to have forfeited rights, and what rights conquerors may claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerogative (executive discretion)
rubrics_metrics.description: This power to act according to discretion, for the public good, without the prescription of the law, and sometimes even against it, is that which is called prerogative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used where the lawmaking power is not always in being or is too slow, and where it is impossible to foresee all accidents and necessities. It allows the executive to do many things of choice which the laws do not prescribe. The key test is whether the action is for the good of the people.

rubrics_metrics.name: When exercise of prerogative is legitimate
rubrics_metrics.description: This power, whilst employed for the benefit of the community, and suitably to the trust and ends of the government, is undoubted prerogative, and never is questioned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The tendency of the exercise of such prerogative 'to the good or hurt of the people' will decide disputes. People seldom examine prerogative while it is tolerably employed for public good; if it manifests harm, it is open to challenge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of executive discretion when law is inadequate
rubrics_metrics.description: Many things there are, which the law can by no means provide for; and those must necessarily be left to the discretion of him that has the executive power in his hands, to be ordered by him as the public good and advantage shall require.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include mitigating the severity of strict laws or pardoning offenders when rigid application would produce harm (e.g., not pulling down an innocent man’s house to stop a fire). The executive should act to preserve as many members of society as possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits and accountability of prerogative
rubrics_metrics.description: People may, by positive laws, define and limit prerogative; doing so is not an encroachment but a clarification of the trust originally left 'in the hands' of the prince for the public good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If rulers use prerogative privately or to promote interests distinct from the public, the people may lawfully claim and limit that power. Historical practice shows prerogative was largest under wise princes but must be checked when misused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedy when no earthly judge exists (appeal to 'heaven')
rubrics_metrics.description: Between an executive power with prerogative and a legislature that depends on his will, there can be no judge on earth; the people have no other remedy but to appeal to heaven.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a body of people is deprived of their right and has no earthly appeal, they retain the ultimate determination to judge whether they have just cause to make an appeal to heaven (i.e., resist or overthrow) when the inconvenience is great and majority feel it. This is constrained by the need for sufficiency of cause and majority discontent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive power to call and organize parliaments as prerogative
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of calling parliaments in England, as to precise time, place, and duration, is certainly a prerogative of the king.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such discretion is justified only insofar as its exercise is 'for the good of the nation,' suitable to exigencies and occasions; the choice should be subservient to the public good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paternal (parental) power — scope and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Paternal or parental power is that which parents have over their children, to govern them for the children’s good, till they come to the use of reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This power is natural and meant for instruction, help, and preservation during minority. It does not extend to life and death over children, nor to holding adult children in subjection once they reach the use of reason; paternal power does not reach the child’s property in full.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political power — origin and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Political power is that power which every man having in the state of nature has given up into the hands of the society, and therein to the governors, with the trust that it shall be employed for their good, and the preservation of their property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Its end and measure are the preservation of lives, liberties, and possessions; it arises from compact/consent and cannot be absolute or arbitrary. Penalties and laws are just insofar as they tend to preserve the whole society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Despotical power — definition and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Despotical power is an absolute, arbitrary power one man has over another, to take away his life, whenever he pleases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This power is not natural nor conveyable by compact; it arises only from forfeiture (e.g., by engaging in a state of war) and applies to captives taken in just and lawful war. Despotical power exceeds political power and is incompatible with civil society except in cases of forfeiture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conquest does not legitimate government without consent
rubrics_metrics.description: Conquest is as far from setting up any government, as demolishing a house is from building a new one in the place. Without the consent of the people, conquest can never erect a new government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Victory in war, even lawful victory, does not by itself confer a legitimate title to govern the conquered people; the consent of those governed remains essential for true political authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights a conqueror legitimately acquires
rubrics_metrics.description: The conqueror gets no power but only over those who have actually assisted, concurred, or consented to that unjust force that is used against him; over those who put themselves in a state of war his power is despotical as to their lives, but he does not thereby have a right to their possessions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A conqueror’s rights are limited to life-forfeiture of aggressors and compensation for damages; he cannot lawfully seize the estates of the innocent (wife and children) or dispossess posterity of inheritance except insofar as necessary to make reparation for war damages and charges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on taking property after conquest
rubrics_metrics.description: The right then of conquest extends only to the lives of those who joined in the war, not to their estates, but only in order to make reparation for the damages received, and the charges of the war, and that too with reservation of the right of the innocent wife and children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where damage is to be repaired, the amount typically cannot justify perpetual dispossession of land; natural law favors preservation of dependents and their shares, and conquerors must yield to pressing maintenance claims of innocents when full satisfaction would leave them to perish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guilt and forfeiture limited to participants
rubrics_metrics.description: He that is guilty of unjust war makes a forfeiture of his life; but this concerns not their children who are in their minority: nor those who did not join in the war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Innocent persons, children, and non-participants do not forfeit rights by the actions of their elders; conquerors have no right to punish or seize from those who have done them no injury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extorted promises and consent invalid
rubrics_metrics.description: Promises extorted by force, without right, bind not at all; whatsoever another gets from me by force, I still retain the right of, and he is obliged presently to restore.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consent obtained under duress (force, threat) is not genuine and imposes no legal or moral obligation; extorted conveyances or promises do not create legitimate title.
